entries.266d8fce3656f33a1d58caa7cbbee69bd5714ec9: <div sID="gen18973" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Ezek.29" sID="Ezek.29"/> <div eID="gen18973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18974" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18975" type="x-p"/> Three chapters we had concerning Tyre and its king; next follow four chapters concerning Egypt and its king. This is the first of them. Egypt had formerly been a house of bondage to God's people; of late they had had but too friendly a correspondence with it, and had depended too much upon it; and therefore, whether the prediction reached Egypt or no, it would be of use to Israel, to take them off from their confidence in their alliance with it. The prophecies against Egypt, which are all laid together in these four chapters, were of five several dates; the first in the 10th year of the captivity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1">ver. 1</reference>), the second in the 27th (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17">ver. 17</reference>), the third in the 11th year and the first month (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20">ch. xxx. 20</reference>), the fourth in the 11th year and the third month (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.1">ch. xxxi. 1</reference>), the fifth in the 12th year (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.1">ch. xxxii. 1</reference>), and another in the same year, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17">ver. 17</reference>. In this chapter we have, I. The destruction of Pharaoh foretold, for his dealing deceitfully with Israel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1-Ezek.29.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. The desolation of the land of Egypt foretold, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.8-Ezek.29.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. III. A promise of the restoration thereof, in part, after forty years, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.13-Ezek.29.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. IV. The possession that should be given to Nebuchadnezzar of the land of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.20">ver. 17-20</reference>. V. A promise of mercy to Israel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.21">ver. 21</reference>.
entries.638b764ad246b8ffad3bb03ac21a67dbeec33d91: <div eID="gen18975" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18974" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Pride of Pharaoh; The Ruin of Pharaoh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen18976" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the tenth year, in the tenth <hi type="italic">month,</hi> in the twelfth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, set thy face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him, and against all Egypt: <hi type="super">3</hi> Speak, and say, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers, which hath said, My river <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine own, and I have made <hi type="italic">it</hi> for myself. <hi type="super">4</hi> But I will put hooks in thy jaws, and I will cause the fish of thy rivers to stick unto thy scales, and I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers, and all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales. <hi type="super">5</hi> And I will leave thee <hi type="italic">thrown</hi> into the wilderness, thee and all the fish of thy rivers: thou shalt fall upon the open fields; thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered: I have given thee for meat to the beasts of the field and to the fowls of the heaven. <hi type="super">6</hi> And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because they have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> When they took hold of thee by thy hand, thou didst break, and rend all their shoulder: and when they leaned upon thee, thou brakest, and madest all their loins to be at a stand. <div eID="gen18976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18977" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The date of this prophecy against Egypt. It was in the <hi type="italic">tenth year of the captivity,</hi> and yet it is placed after the prophecy against Tyre, which was delivered in the eleventh year, because, in the accomplishment of the prophecies, the destruction of Tyre happened before the destruction of Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar's gaining Egypt was the reward of his service against Tyre; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the prophecy against Tyre is put first, that we may the better observe that. But particular notice must be taken of this, that the first prophecy against Egypt was just at the time when the king of Egypt was coming to relieve Jerusalem and raise the siege (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jer. xxxvii. 5</reference>), but did not answer the expectations of the Jews from them. Note, It is good to foresee the failing of all our creature-confidences, then when we are most in temptation to depend upon them, that we may <hi type="italic">cease from man.</hi> <div eID="gen18977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18978" type="x-p"/> II. The scope of this prophecy. It is directed against <hi type="italic">Pharaoh king of Egypt, and against all Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.2">v. 2</reference>. The prophecy against Tyre began with the people, and then proceeded against the prince. But this begins with the prince, because it began to have its accomplishment in the insurrections and rebellions of the people against the prince, not long after this. <div eID="gen18978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18979" type="x-p"/> III. The prophecy itself. Pharaoh Hophrah (for so was the reigning Pharaoh surnamed) is here represented by a <hi type="italic">great dragon,</hi> or crocodile, that <hi type="italic">lies in the midst of his rivers,</hi> as Leviathan in the waters, to <hi type="italic">play therein,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">v. 3</reference>. Nilus, the river of Egypt, was famed for crocodiles. And what is the king of Egypt, in God's account, but a <hi type="italic">great dragon,</hi> venomous and mischievous? Therefore says God, <hi type="italic">I am against thee. I am above thee;</hi> so it may be read. How high soever the princes and potentates of the earth are, there is a <hi type="italic">higher than they</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Eccl. v. 8</reference>), a God above them, that can control them, and, if they be tyrannical and oppressive, a God against them, that will be free to reckon with them. Observe here, <div eID="gen18979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18980" type="x-p"/> 1. The pride and security of Pharaoh. He <hi type="italic">lies in the midst of his rivers,</hi> rolls himself with a great deal of satisfaction in his wealth and pleasures; and he says, <hi type="italic">My river is my own.</hi> He boasts that he is an absolute prince (his subjects are his vassals; Joseph bought them long ago, <reference osisRef="Gen.47.23">Gen. xlvii. 23</reference>),—that he is a sole prince, and has neither partner in the government nor competitor for it,—that he is out of debt (what he has is his <hi type="italic">own,</hi> and none of his neighbours have any demands upon him),—that he is independent, neither tributary nor accountable to any. Note, Worldly carnal minds please themselves with, and pride themselves in, their property, forgetting that whatever we have we have only the use of it, the property is in God. We ourselves are not our own, but his. Our <hi type="italic">tongues are not our own,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.12.4">Ps. xii. 4</reference>. Our river is not <hi type="italic">our own,</hi> for its springs are in God. The most potent prince cannot call what he has his own, for, though it be so against all the world, it is not so against God. But Pharaoh's reason for his pretensions is yet more absurd: <hi type="italic">My river is my own,</hi> for <hi type="italic">I have made it for myself.</hi> Here he usurps two of the divine prerogatives, to be the author and the end of his own being and felicity. He only that is the great Creator can say of this world, and of every thing in it, <hi type="italic">I have made it for myself.</hi> He calls his river his own because he <hi type="italic">looks not unto the Maker thereof, nor has respect unto him that fashioned it long ago,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa. xxii. 11</reference>. What we have we have received from God and must use for God, so that we cannot say, We made it, much less, We made it for ourselves; and why then do we boast? Note, Self is the great idol that all the world worships, in contempt of God and his sovereignty. <div eID="gen18980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18981" type="x-p"/> 2. The course God will take with this proud man, to humble him. He is a great dragon in the waters, and God will accordingly deal with him, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4-Ezek.29.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. (1.) He will draw him out of his rivers, for he has <hi type="italic">a hook and a cord</hi> for this <hi type="italic">leviathan,</hi> with which he can manage him, though none on earth can (<reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job xli. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers,</hi> will cast thee out of thy palace, out of thy kingdom, out of all those things in which thou takest such a complacency and placest such a confidence." Herodotus related of this Pharaoh, who was now king of Egypt, that he had reigned in great prosperity for twenty-five years, and was so elevated with his successes that he said that <hi type="italic">God himself would not cast him out of his kingdom;</hi> but he shall soon be convinced of his mistake, and what he depended on shall be no defence. God can force men out of that in which they are most secure and easy. (2.) <hi type="italic">All his fish</hi> shall be drawn out with him, his servants, his soldiers, and all that had a dependence on him, as he thought, but really such as he had dependence upon. These shall <hi type="italic">stick to his scales,</hi> adhere to their king, resolving to live and die with him. But, (3.) The king and his army, the dragon and all the fish that stick to his scales, shall perish together, as fish cast upon dry ground, and shall be <hi type="italic">meat to the beasts and fowls,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5">v. 5</reference>. Now this is supposed to have had its accomplishment soon after, when this Pharaoh, in defence of Aricius king of Libya, who had been expelled his kingdom by the Cyrenians, levied a great army, and went out against the Cyrenians, to re-establish his friend, but was defeated in battle, and all his forces were put to flight, which gave such disgust to his kingdom that they rose in rebellion against him. Thus was he left <hi type="italic">thrown into the wilderness, he and all the fish of the river</hi> with him. Thus issue men's pride, and presumption, and carnal security. Thus men justly lose what they might call their own, under God, when they call it their own against him. <div eID="gen18981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18982" type="x-p"/> 3. The ground of the controversy God has with the Egyptians; it is because they have cheated his people. They encouraged them to expect relief and assistance from them when they were in distress, but failed them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.6-Ezek.29.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because they have been a staff of reed to the house of</hi> Israel. They pretended to be a staff for them to lean upon, but, when any stress was laid upon them, they were either weak and could not or treacherous and would not do that for them which was expected. They <hi type="italic">broke under them,</hi> to their great disappointment and amazement, so that they <hi type="italic">rent their shoulder</hi> and <hi type="italic">made all their loins to be at a stand.</hi> The king of Egypt, it is probable, had encouraged Zedekiah to break his league with the king of Babylon, with a promise that he would stand by him, which, when he failed to do, to any purpose, it could not but put them into a great consternation. God had told them, long since, that the Egyptians were broken reeds, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa. xxx. 6, 7</reference>. Rabshakeh had told them so, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">Isa. xxxvi. 6</reference>. And now they found it so. It was indeed the folly of Israel to trust them, and they were well enough served when they were deceived in them. God was righteous in suffering them to be so. But that is no excuse at all for the Egyptians' falsehood and treachery, nor shall it secure them from the judgments of that God who is and will be the avenger of all such wrongs. It is a great sin, and very provoking to God, as well as unjust, ungrateful, and very dishonourable and unkind, to put a cheat upon those that put a confidence in us.
entries.58357e2c4148cbdf9e32c44eb06007b710c8c7d4: <div eID="gen18982" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Fall and Restoration of Egypt. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen18983" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I will bring a sword upon thee, and cut off man and beast out of thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : because he hath said, The river <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, and I have made <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> Behold, therefore I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, and against thy rivers, and I will make the land of Egypt utterly waste <hi type="italic">and</hi> desolate, from the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia. <hi type="super">11</hi> No foot of man shall pass through it, nor foot of beast shall pass through it, neither shall it be inhabited forty years. <hi type="super">12</hi> And I will make the land of Egypt desolate in the midst of the countries <hi type="italic">that are</hi> desolate, and her cities among the cities <hi type="italic">that are</hi> laid waste shall be desolate forty years: and I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries. <hi type="super">13</hi> Yet thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; At the end of forty years will I gather the Egyptians from the people whither they were scattered: <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will bring again the captivity of Egypt, and will cause them to return <hi type="italic">into</hi> the land of Pathros, into the land of their habitation; and they shall be there a base kingdom. <hi type="super">15</hi> It shall be the basest of the kingdoms; neither shall it exalt itself any more above the nations: for I will diminish them, that they shall no more rule over the nations. <hi type="super">16</hi> And it shall be no more the confidence of the house of Israel, which bringeth <hi type="italic">their</hi> iniquity to remembrance, when they shall look after them: but they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18984" type="x-p"/> This explains the foregoing prediction, which was figurative, and looks something further. Here is a prophecy, <div eID="gen18984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18985" type="x-p"/> I. Of the ruin of Egypt. The threatening of this is very full and particular; and the sin for which this ruin shall be brought upon them is their pride, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.9">v. 9</reference>. They said, <hi type="italic">The river is mine and I have made it;</hi> therefore their land shall spue them out. 1. God is against them, both against the king and against the people, <hi type="italic">against thee and against thy rivers.</hi> Waters signify <hi type="italic">people and multitudes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Rev. xvii. 15</reference>. 2. Multitudes of them shall be cut off by the sword of war, a sword which God will bring upon them to destroy <hi type="italic">both man and beast,</hi> the sword of civil war. 3. The country shall be depopulated. The <hi type="italic">land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.9">v. 9</reference>), the country not cultivated, the cities not inhabited. The wealth of both was their pride, and that God will take away. It <hi type="italic">shall be utterly waste (wastes of waste,</hi> so the margin reads it), <hi type="italic">and desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">v. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">neither men nor beasts shall pass through it, nor shall it be inhabited</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.11">v. 11</reference>); it shall be <hi type="italic">desolate in the midst of the countries that are so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.12">v. 12</reference>. This was the effect not so much of those wars spoken of before, which were made by them, but of the war which the king of Babylon made upon them. It shall be desolate from one end of the land to the other, <hi type="italic">from the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia.</hi> The sin of pride is enough to ruin a whole nation. 4. The people shall be dispersed and scattered among the nations (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.12">v. 12</reference>), so that those who thought the balance of power was in their hand should now become a contemptible people. Such a fall does a haughty spirit go before. <div eID="gen18985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18986" type="x-p"/> II. Of the restoration of Egypt after awhile, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.13">v. 13</reference>. Egypt shall lie <hi type="italic">desolate forty years</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.12">v. 12</reference>) and then <hi type="italic">I will bring again the captivity of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.14">v. 14</reference>. Some date the forty years from Nebuchadnezzar's destroying Egypt, others from the desolation of Egypt some time before; however, they end about the first year of Cyrus, when the seventy years' captivity of Judah ended, or soon after. Then this prediction was accomplished, 1. That God will gather the Egyptians out of all the countries into which they were dispersed, and make them to <hi type="italic">return to the land of their habitation,</hi> and give them a settlement there again, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.14">v. 14</reference>. Note, Though God will find out a way to humble the proud, yet he will not contend for ever, no, not with them in this world. 2. That yet they shall not make a figure again as they have done. Egypt shall be <hi type="italic">a kingdom</hi> again, but it shall be the <hi type="italic">basest of the kingdoms</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.15">v. 15</reference>); it shall have but little wealth and power, and shall not extend its conquests as formerly; it shall be the tail of the nations, and not the head. It is a mercy that it shall become a kingdom again, but, to humble it, it shall be a despicable kingdom; it shall be a long time before it recover any thing like its ancient lustre. For two reasons it shall be thus mortified:—(1.) That it may not domineer over its neighbours, that it may not <hi type="italic">exalt itself above the nations,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">rule over the nations,</hi> as it has done, but that it may know what it is to be low and despised. Note, Those who abuse their power will justly be stripped of it; and God, as King of nations, will find out a way to maintain the injured rights and liberties, not only of his own, but of other nations. (2.) That it may not deceive the people of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">It shall no more be the confidence of the house of Israel;</hi> they shall no more be in temptation to trust in it as they have done, which is a sin that <hi type="italic">brings their iniquity to remembrance,</hi> that is, provokes God to punish them not for that only, but for all their other sins. Or it <hi type="italic">puts them in mind</hi> of their idolatries to return to them, <hi type="italic">when they look</hi> to the idolaters, to repose a confidence in them. Note, The creatures we confide in are often <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> ruined, because there is no other way effectually to cure us of our confidence in them. Rather than Israel shall be ensnared again, the whole land of Egypt shall be laid waste. He that once <hi type="italic">gave Egypt for their ransom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.3">Isa. xliii. 3</reference>) will now give Egypt for their cure; and it shall be destroyed rather than Israel shall not in this particular be reformed. God, not only in justice, but in wisdom and goodness to us, breaks those creature-stays which we lean too much upon, and makes them to be no more, that they may be no more our confidence.
entries.a0c2300a804b15ac811837ac57e25533d4f7cc35: <div eID="gen18986" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Promise to Nebuchadnezzar. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen18987" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And it came to pass in the seven and twentieth year, in the first <hi type="italic">month,</hi> in the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">18</hi> Son of man, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus: every head <hi type="italic">was</hi> made bald, and every shoulder <hi type="italic">was</hi> peeled: yet had he no wages, nor his army, for Tyrus, for the service that he had served against it: <hi type="super">19</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude, and take her spoil, and take her prey; and it shall be the wages for his army. <hi type="super">20</hi> I have given him the land of Egypt <hi type="italic">for</hi> his labour wherewith he served against it, because they wrought for me, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">21</hi> In that day will I cause the horn of the house of Israel to bud forth, and I will give thee the opening of the mouth in the midst of them; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18988" type="x-p"/> The date of this prophecy is observable; it was in the twenty-seventh year of Ezekiel's captivity, sixteen years after the prophecy in the former part of the chapter, and almost as long after those which follow in the next chapters; but it comes in here for the explication of all that was said against Egypt. After the destruction of Jerusalem Nebuchadnezzar spent two or three campaigns in the conquest of the Ammonites and Moabites and making himself master of their countries. Then he spent thirteen years in the siege of Tyre. During all that time the Egyptians were embroiled in war with the Cyrenians and one with another, by which they were very much weakened and impoverished; and just at the end of the siege of Tyre God delivers this prophecy to Ezekiel, to signify to him that that utter destruction of Egypt which he had foretold fifteen or sixteen years before, which had been but in part accomplished hitherto, should now be completed by Nebuchadnezzar. The prophecy which begins here, it should seem, is continued to the <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20">twentieth verse</reference> of the next chapter. And Dr. Lightfoot observes that it is the last prophecy we have of this prophet, and should have been last in the book, but is laid here, that all the prophecies against Egypt might come together. The particular destruction of Pharaoh-Hophrah, foretold in the former part of this chapter, was likewise foretold <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">Jer. xliv. 30</reference>. This general devastation of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar was foretold <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10">Jer. xliii. 10</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen18988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18989" type="x-p"/> I. What success God would give to Nebuchadnezzar and his forces against Egypt. God gave him <hi type="italic">that land,</hi> that he might <hi type="italic">take the spoil</hi> and <hi type="italic">prey</hi> of it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.19-Ezek.29.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. It was a cheap and easy prey. He subdued it with very little difficulty; the blood and treasure expended upon the conquest of it were inconsiderable. But it was a rich prey, and he carried off a great deal from it that was of value. Their having been divided among themselves, no doubt, gave a common enemy great advantage against them, who, when they had been so long preying upon one another, soon made a prey of them all. <hi type="italic">En! quo discordia cives perduxit miseros—What wretchedness does civil discord bring!</hi> Jeremiah foretold that Nebuchadnezzar should <hi type="italic">array himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd puts on his coat,</hi> which intimates what a rich and cheap prey it should be. <div eID="gen18989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18990" type="x-p"/> II. Upon what considerations God would give Nebuchadnezzar this success against Egypt; it was to be a recompence to him for the hard service with which he had caused his army to serve against Tyre, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18">v. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.20">20</reference>. 1. The taking of Tyre was a tedious piece of work; it cost Nebuchadnezzar abundance of blood and treasure. It held out thirteen years; all that time the Chaldean army was hard at it, to make themselves masters of it. A large current of the sea, between Tyre and the continent, was filled up with earth, and many other difficulties which were thought insuperable they had to struggle with; but so great a prince, having begun such an undertaking, thought himself bound in honour to push it on, whatever it cost him. How many thousand lives have been sacrificed to such points of honour as this as! In prosecuting this siege <hi type="italic">every head was made bald, and every shoulder peeled,</hi> with carrying burdens and labouring in the water when they had a strong tide and a strong town to contend with. Egypt, a large kingdom, being divided within itself, is easily conquered; Tyre, a single city, being unanimous, is with difficulty subdued. Those that have much to do in the world find some affairs go on a great deal more readily and easily than others. But, 2. In this service God own that they <hi type="italic">wrought for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.20">v. 20</reference>. He set them at work, for the humbling of a proud city and its king, though <hi type="italic">they meant not so, neither did their heart think so,</hi> who were employed in it. Note, Even great men and bad men are tools that God makes use of, and are <hi type="italic">working for him</hi> even when they are pursuing their own covetous and ambitious designs; so wonderfully does God overrule all to his own glory. Yet, 3. For this service he had <hi type="italic">no wages</hi> nor <hi type="italic">his army.</hi> He was at a vast expense to take Tyre; and when he had it, though it was a very rich city, and he promised himself good plunder for his army from it, he was disappointed; the Tyrians sent away by ship their best effects, and threw the rest into the sea, so that they had nothing but bare walls. Thus are the children of this world ordinarily frustrated in their highest expectations from it. Therefore, 4. He shall have the spoil of Egypt to recompense him for his service against Tyre. Note, God will be behind-hand with none for any service they do for him, but, one way or other, will recompense them for it; none shall kindle a fire on his altar for nought. The service done for him by worldly men, with worldly designs, shall be recompensed with a mere worldly reward, which his faithful servants, that have a sincere regard to his will and glory, would not be put off with. This accounts for the prosperity of wicked men in this world; God is in it paying them for some service or other, in which he has made use of them. <hi type="italic">Verily they have their reward.</hi> Let none envy it them. The conquest of Egypt is spoken of as Nebuchadnezzar's <hi type="italic">full reward,</hi> for that completed his dominion over the then known world in a manner; that was the last of the kingdoms he subdued; when he was master of that he became the <hi type="italic">head of gold.</hi> <div eID="gen18990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18991" type="x-p"/> III. The mercy God had in store for the house of Israel soon after. When the tide is at the highest it will turn, and so it will when it is at the lowest. Nebuchadnezzar was in the zenith of his glory when he had conquered Egypt, but within a year after he ran mad (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.28-Dan.4.37">Dan. iv.</reference>), was so seven years, and within a year or two after he had recovered his senses he resigned his life. When he was at the highest Israel was at the lowest; then were they in the depth of their captivity, their bones dead and dry; but <hi type="italic">in that day the horn of the house of Israel shall bud forth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.21">v. 21</reference>. The day of their deliverance shall begin to dawn, and they shall have some little reviving in their bondage, in the honour that shall be done, 1. To their princes; they are the <hi type="italic">horns of the house of Israel,</hi> the seat of their glory and power. These began to bud forth when Daniel and his fellows were highly preferred in Babylon; Daniel <hi type="italic">sat in the gate of the city; Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, were set over the affairs of the province</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.49">Dan. ii. 49</reference>); these were all <hi type="italic">of the king's seed, and of the princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.1.3">Dan. i. 3</reference>. And it was within a year after the conquest of Egypt that they were thus preferred; and, soon after, three of them were made famous by the honour God put upon them in bringing them alive out of the burning fiery furnace. This might very well be called the <hi type="italic">budding forth of the horn of the house of Israel.</hi> And, some years after, this promise had a further accomplishment in the enlargement and elevation of Jehoiachin king of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31-Jer.52.32">Jer. lii. 31, 32</reference>. They were both tokens of God's favour to Israel, and happy omens. 2. To their prophets. And <hi type="italic">I will give thee the opening of the mouth.</hi> Though none of Ezekiel's prophecies, after this, are recorded, yet we have reason to think he went on prophesying, and with more liberty and boldness, when Daniel and his fellows were in power, and would be ready to protect him not only from the Babylonians, but from the wicked ones of his own people. Note, It bodes well to a people when God enlarges the liberties of his ministers and they are countenanced and encouraged in their work.  <chapter eID="Ezek.29"/> <div eID="gen18991" type="x-p"/>

entries.786e9b41df0f97573bef4c42fc7ca0511427e034: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11572"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1-Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:1-21</reference>. The Judgment on Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar; though about to Be Restored after Forty Years, It Was Still to Be in a State of Degradation.</title> <div sID="gen20970" type="x-p"/> This is the last of the world kingdoms against which Ezekiel's prophecies are directed, and occupies the largest space in them, namely, the next four chapters. Though farther off than Tyre, it exercised a more powerful influence on Israel.<div eID="gen20970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11572"/><hi type="bold">2. Pharaoh--</hi>a common name of all the kings of Egypt, meaning "the sun"; or, as others say, a "crocodile," which was worshipped in parts of Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>). Hophra or Apries was on the throne at this time. His reign began prosperously. He took Gaza (<reference osisRef="Jer.47.1">Jr 47:1</reference>) and Zidon and made himself master of Phoenicia and Palestine, recovering much that was lost to Egypt by the victory of Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>), in the fourth year of Jehoiakim [Wilkinson, Ancient Egypt, 1.169]. So proudly secure because of his successes for twenty-five years did he feel, that he said not even a god could deprive him of his kingdom [Herodotus, 2.169]. Hence the appropriateness of the description of him in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>. No mere human sagacity could have enabled Ezekiel to foresee Egypt's downfall in the height of its prosperity. There are four divisions of these prophecies; the first in the tenth year of Ezekiel's captivity; the last in the twelfth. Between the first and second comes one of much later date, not having been given till the twenty-seventh year (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17">Eze 29:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.19">30:19</reference>), but placed there as appropriate to the subject matter. Pharaoh-hophra, or Apries, was dethroned and strangled, and Amasis substituted as king, by Nebuchadnezzar (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">Jr 44:30</reference>). The Egyptian priests, from national vanity, made no mention to Herodotus of the Egyptian loss of territory in Syria through Nebuchadnezzar, of which Josephus tells us, but attributed the change in the succession from Apries to Amasis solely to the Egyptian soldiery. The civil war between the two rivals no doubt lasted several years, affording an opportunity to Nebuchadnezzar of interfering and of elevating the usurper Amasis, on condition of his becoming tributary to Babylon [Wilkinson]. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10-Jer.43.12">Jr 43:10-12</reference>, and see on <reference osisRef="Jer.43.13">Jr 43:13</reference>, for another view of the grounds of interference of Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen20971" type="x-p"/>
entries.05ce66c6a4c3004d637fa1fa81ee02b2c8f83908: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11573"/><div sID="gen20972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11573"/><hi type="bold">3. dragon--</hi>Hebrew, tanim, any large aquatic animal, here the crocodile, which on Roman coins is the emblem of Egypt.<div eID="gen20972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lieth--</hi>restest proudly secure.<div eID="gen20973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his rivers--</hi>the mouths, branches, and canals of the Nile, to which Egypt owed its fertility. <div eID="gen20974" type="x-p"/>
entries.79ad5fb561deca0fe6e119af49e2b355eabd0b69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11574"/><div sID="gen20975" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11574"/><hi type="bold">4. hooks in thy jaws--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Is 37:29</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference>, 2). Amasis was the "hook." In the Assyrian sculptures prisoners are represented with a hook in the underlip, and a cord from it held by the king.<div eID="gen20975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cause ... fish ... stick unto ... scales--</hi>Pharaoh, presuming on his power as if he were God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>, "I have made it"), wished to stand in the stead of God as defender of the covenant-people, his motive being, not love to them, but rivalry with Babylon. He raised the siege of Jerusalem, but it was only for a time (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.6">Eze 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7-Jer.37.10">7-10</reference>); ruin overtook not only them, but himself. As the fish that clung to the horny scales of the crocodile, the lord of the Nile, when he was caught, shared his fate, so the adherents of Pharaoh, lord of Egypt, when he was overthrown by Amasis, should share his fate. <div eID="gen20976" type="x-p"/>
entries.63576a518ceea2dfb58c82444b571ddcf09de367: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11575"/><div sID="gen20977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11575"/><hi type="bold">5. wilderness--</hi>captivity beyond thy kingdom. The expression is used perhaps to imply retribution in kind. As Egypt pursued after Israel, saying, "The wilderness hath shut them in" (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.3">Ex 14:3</reference>), so she herself shall be brought into a wilderness state.<div eID="gen20977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">open fields--</hi>literally, "face of the field."<div eID="gen20978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not be brought together--</hi>As the crocodile is not, when caught, restored to the river, so no remnant of thy routed army shall be brought together, and rallied, after its defeat in the wilderness. Pharaoh led an army against Cyrene in Africa, in support of Aricranes, who had been stripped of his kingdom by the Cyrenians. The army perished and Egypt rebelled against him [Junius]. But the reference is mainly to the defeat by Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen20979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beasts ... fowls--</hi>hostile and savage men. <div eID="gen20980" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfea5aa3f989e503900bb859af08f5cea9607a4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11576"/><div sID="gen20981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11576"/><hi type="bold">6. staff of reed to ... Israel--</hi>alluding to the reeds on the banks of the Nile, which broke if one leaned upon them (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4">Eze 29:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">Is 36:6</reference>). All Israel's dependence on Egypt proved hurtful instead of beneficial (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.1-Isa.30.5">Is 30:1-5</reference>). <div eID="gen20981" type="x-p"/>
entries.e879b7ec719292c129e8f6bb66e4f2ef8fa19b4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11577"/><div sID="gen20982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11577"/><hi type="bold">7. hand--</hi>or handle of the reed.<div eID="gen20982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rend ... shoulder--</hi>by the splinters on which the shoulder or arm would fall, on the support failing the hand.<div eID="gen20983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">madest ... loins ... at a stand--</hi>that is, made them to be disabled. Maurer somewhat similarly (referring to a kindred Arabic form), "Thou hast stricken both their loins." Fairbairn, not so well, "Thou lettest all their loins stand," that is, by themselves, bereft of the support which they looked for from thee. <div eID="gen20984" type="x-p"/>
entries.5030b3054b23b0f9b356baa86df4fb86750082c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11578"/><div sID="gen20985" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11578"/><hi type="bold">8. a sword--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar's army (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.19">Eze 29:19</reference>). Also Amasis and the Egyptian revolters who after Pharaoh-hophra's discomfiture in Cyrene dethroned and strangled him, having defeated him in a battle fought at Memphis [Junius]. <div eID="gen20985" type="x-p"/>
entries.1dec7ac52a121a1a039b5f5a8f8eb8ec3deb9a15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11579"/><div sID="gen20986" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11579"/><hi type="bold">9. I am the Lord--</hi>in antithesis to the blasphemous boast repeated here from <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>, "The river is mine, and I have made it." <div eID="gen20986" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9e3eefd0697576e63b1d3b351d0a8e029ba58ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11580"/><div sID="gen20987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11580"/><hi type="bold">10. from the tower of Syene--</hi>Grotius translates, "from Migdol (a fortress near Pelusium on the north of Suez) to Syene (in the farthest south)"; that is, from one end of Egypt to the other. So "from Migdol to Syene," <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">Eze 30:6</reference>, Margin. However, English Version rightly refers Syene to Seveneh, that is, Sebennytus, in the eastern delta of the Nile, the capital of the Lower Egyptian kings. The Sebennyte Pharaohs, with the help of the Canaanites, who, as shepherds or merchants, ranged the desert of Suez, extended their borders beyond the narrow province east of the delta, to which they had been confined by the Pharaohs of Upper Egypt. The defeated party, in derision, named the Sebennyte or Lower Egyptians foreigners and shepherd-kings (a shepherd being an abomination in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.46.34">Ge 46:34</reference>). They were really a native dynasty. Thus, in English Version, "Ethiopia" in the extreme south is rightly contrasted with Sebennytus or Syene in the north. <div eID="gen20987" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fff924a952f4e6561ac89fb48d3f8fcc788711a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11581"/><div sID="gen20988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11581"/><hi type="bold">11. forty years--</hi>answering to the forty years in which the Israelites, their former bondsmen, wandered in "the wilderness" (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:5</reference>). Jerome remarks the number forty is one often connected with affliction and judgment. The rains of the flood in forty days brought destruction on the world. Moses, Elias, and the Saviour fasted forty days. The interval between Egypt's overthrow by Nebuchadnezzar and the deliverance by Cyrus, was about forty years. The ideal forty years' wilderness state of social and political degradation, rather than a literal non-passing of man or beast for that term, is mainly intended (so <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.6">Eze 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Is 19:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen20988" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2860d91ee7190befd75ab156f135fa0cf644d05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11582"/><div sID="gen20989" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11582"/>12. As Israel passed through a term of wilderness discipline (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.35">Eze 20:35</reference>, &c.), which was in its essential features to be repeated again, so it was to be with Egypt [Fairbairn]. Some Egyptians were to be carried to Babylon, also many "scattered" in Arabia and Ethiopia through fear; but mainly the "scattering" was to be the dissipation of their power, even though the people still remained in their own land. <div eID="gen20989" type="x-p"/>
entries.443e041eb459d99aa8505b0de19f6b6248bd3ac0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11583"/><div sID="gen20990" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11583"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.26">Jr 46:26</reference>). <div eID="gen20990" type="x-p"/>
entries.c482471f73f7e680f08df869ab92dfbc957083d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11584"/><div sID="gen20991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11584"/><hi type="bold">14. Pathros--</hi>the Thebaid, or Upper Egypt, which had been especially harassed by Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Na 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.10">10</reference>). The oldest part of Egypt as to civilization and art. The Thebaid was anciently called "Egypt" [Aristotle]. Therefore it is called the "land of the Egyptians' birth" (Margin, for "habitation").<div eID="gen20991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">base kingdom--</hi>Under Amasis it was made dependent on Babylon; humbled still more under Cambyses; and though somewhat raised under the Ptolemies, never has it regained its ancient pre-eminence. <div eID="gen20992" type="x-p"/>
entries.edeb743f2a54b6e60fb26b3bd823db96d4ec14b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11585"/><div sID="gen20993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11585"/>16. Egypt, when restored, shall be so circumscribed in power that it shall be no longer an object of confidence to Israel, as formerly; for example, as when, relying on it, Israel broke faith with Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.13">Eze 17:13</reference>, 15, 16).<div eID="gen20993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which bringeth their iniquity to remembrance, when they shall look after them--</hi>rather, "while they (the Israelites) look to (or, turn after) them" [Henderson]. Israel's looking to Egypt, rather than to God, causes their iniquity (unfaithfulness to the covenant) to be remembered by God. <div eID="gen20994" type="x-p"/>
entries.5711c950e6fd6a3ace82d3abfd45cff43af99586: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11586"/><div sID="gen20995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11586"/>17. The departure from the chronological order occurs here only, among the prophecies as to foreign nations, in order to secure greater unity of subject. <div eID="gen20995" type="x-p"/>
entries.7554f599bc2a2ab20b41f1287760fe5f932b6524: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11587"/><div sID="gen20996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11587"/><hi type="bold">18. every head ... bald, ... shoulder ... peeled--</hi>with carrying baskets of earth and stones for the siege works.<div eID="gen20996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no wages ... for the service--</hi>that is, in proportion to it and the time and labor which he expended on the siege of Tyre. Not that he actually failed in the siege (Jerome expressly states, from Assyrian histories, that Nebuchadnezzar succeeded); but, so much of the Tyrian resources had been exhausted, or transported to her colonies in ships, that little was left to compensate Nebuchadnezzar for his thirteen year's siege. <div eID="gen20997" type="x-p"/>
entries.aca445fa003e9dcaadcceece5d06b30a8ba0c207: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11588"/><div sID="gen20998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11588"/><hi type="bold">19. multitude--</hi>not as Fairbairn, "store"; but, he shall take away a multitude of captives out of Egypt. The success of Nebuchadnezzar is implied in Tyre's receiving a king from Babylon, probably one of her captives there, Merbal.<div eID="gen20998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take her spoil ... prey--</hi>literally, "spoil her spoil, prey her prey," that is, as she spoiled other nations, so shall she herself be a spoil to Babylon. <div eID="gen20999" type="x-p"/>
entries.b56a378fd427243a7fd632ec36ba63784f54a976: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11589"/><div sID="gen21000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11589"/><hi type="bold">20. because they wrought for me--</hi>the Chaldeans, fulfilling My will as to Tyre (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9">Jr 25:9</reference>). <div eID="gen21000" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bf21080fac01d0c924b21ae96f5c09a2eb3e78b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11590"/><div sID="gen21001" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11590"/>21. In the evil only, not in the good, was Egypt to be parallel to Israel. The very downfall of Egypt will be the signal for the rise of Israel, because of God's covenant with the latter.<div eID="gen21001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I cause the horn of ... Israel to bud--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Psa 132:17</reference>). I will cause its ancient glory to revive: an earnest of Israel's full glory under Messiah, the son of David (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">Lu 1:69</reference>). Even in Babylon an earnest was given of this in Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.2">Da 6:2</reference>) and Jeconiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.31">Jr 52:31</reference>).<div eID="gen21002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will give thee ... opening of ... mouth--</hi>When thy predictions shall have come to pass, thy words henceforth shall be more heeded (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.27">Eze 24:27</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.29"/>

entries.aba21fb19eb44fbbf631b5534742bfcfd89db068: <div eID="gen32123" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32124" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32125" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32125" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32124" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32126" type="x-p"/> This and the three following chapters foretell the conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar, which he accomplished in the twenty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity. The same event is foretold by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13">Jer 46:13</reference>, etc. The prophecy opens with God's charging the king of Egypt (Pharaoh-hophra) with the same extravagant pride and profanity which were in the preceding chapter laid to the charge of the prince of Tyre. He appears, like him, to have affected Divine honors; and boasted so much of the strength of his kingdom, that, as an ancient historian (Herodotus) tells us, he impiously declared that God himself could not dispossess him. Wherefore the prophet, with great majesty, addresses him under the image of one of those crocodiles or monsters which inhabited that river, of whose riches and revenue he vaunted; and assures him that, with as much ease as a fisherman drags the fish he has hooked, God would drag him and his people into captivity, and that their carcasses should fall a prey to the beasts of the field and to the fowls of heaven, <reference osisRef="Eze.29.1-Eze.29.7">Eze 29:1-7</reference>. The figure is then dropped; and God is introduced denouncing, in plain terns, the most awful judgments against him and his nation, and declaring that the Egyptians should be subjected to the Babylonians till the fall of the Chaldean empire, <reference osisRef="Eze.29.8-Eze.29.12">Eze 29:8-12</reference>. The prophet then foretells that Egypt, which was about to be devastated by the Babylonians, and many of the people carried into captivity, should again become a kingdom; but that it should never regain its ancient political importance; for, in the lapse of time, it should be even the Basest of the kingdoms, a circumstance in the prophecy most literally fulfilled, especially under the Christian dispensation, in its government by the Mameluke slaves, <reference osisRef="Eze.29.13-Eze.29.16">Eze 29:13-16</reference>. The prophecy, beginning at the seventeenth verse, is connected with the foregoing, as it relates to the same subject, though delivered about seventeen years later. Nebuchadnezzar and his army, after the long siege of Tyre, which made every head bald by constantly wearing their helmets, and wore the skin of off every shoulder by carrying burdens to raise the fortifications, were disappointed of the spoil which they expected, by the retiring of the inhabitants to Carthage. God, therefore, promises him Egypt for his reward, <reference osisRef="Eze.29.17-Eze.29.20">Eze 29:17-20</reference>. The chapter concludes with a prediction of the return of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, <reference osisRef="Eze.29.21">Eze 29:21</reference>. <div eID="gen32126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32127" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32128" type="x-p"/> In the tenth year - Of Zedekiah; and tenth of the captivity of Jeconiah. <div eID="gen32128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32129" type="x-p"/> The ten month, in the twelfth day of the month - Answering to Monday, the first of February, A.M. 3415.
entries.7b051d4c8dcd36c3dbf3c9463e20f8d4881769a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32130" type="x-p"/> Set thy face against Pharaoh king of Egypt - This was Pharaoh-hophra or Pharaoh-apries, whom we have so frequently met with in the prophecies of Jeremiah, and much of whose history has been given in the notes.
entries.f9384625c5dd60eb5c128e3e8dbe68fc88ce05a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen32130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32131" type="x-p"/> The great dragon - התנים hattannim should here be translated crocodile, as that is a real animal, and numerous in the Nile; whereas the dragon is wholly fabulous. The original signifies any large animal. <div eID="gen32131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32132" type="x-p"/> The midst of his rivers - This refers to the several branches of the Nile, by which this river empties itself into the Mediterranean. The ancients termed them septem ostia Nili, "the seven mouths of the Nile." The crocodile was the emblem of Egypt.
entries.0f2175b763f7a55c1cb54ebd1e0c74d615689ced: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32133" type="x-p"/> I will put hooks in thy jaws - Amasis, one of this king's generals, being proclaimed king by an insurrection of the people, dethroned Apries, and seized upon the kingdom; and Apries was obliged to flee to Upper Egypt for safety. <div eID="gen32133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32134" type="x-p"/> I will cause the fish - to stick unto thy scales - Most fish are sorely troubled with a species of insect which bury their heads in their flesh, under their scales, and suck out the vital juices. The allusion seems to be to this. Pharaoh was the crocodile; the fish, the common people; and the sticking to his scales, the insurrection by which he was wasted and despoiled of his kingdom.
entries.baf0c9e3a76ecb13d71d2a1c9716df4f547db3b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32135" type="x-p"/> I will leave thee thrown into the wilderness - Referring to his being obliged to take refuge in Upper Egypt. But he was afterwards taken prisoner, and strangled by Amasis. Herod. lib. 2 s. 169.
entries.8d787f2b14249d898f540522e82595b9e1524488: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen32135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32136" type="x-p"/> They have been a staff of reed - An inefficient and faithless ally. The Israelites expected assistance from them when Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem; and they made a feint to help them, but retired when Nebuchadnezzar went against them. Thus were the Jews deceived and ultimately ruined, see <reference osisRef="Eze.29.7">Eze 29:7</reference>.
entries.cfb5c3b44876c6c890540f88b953eae774eeb081: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32137" type="x-p"/> From the tower of Syene - ממגדל מונה mimmigdol seveneh, "from Migdol to Syene." Syene, now called Essuan, was the last city in Egypt, going towards Ethiopia. It was famous for a well into which the rays of the sun fell perpendicularly at midday.
entries.6cbd419b1a2a041cc01c6b6d42aae6202aaa5d01: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen32137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32138" type="x-p"/> Shall be desolate forty years - The country from Migdol or Magdolan, which was on the isthmus between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, was so completely ruined, that it might well be called desert; and it is probable that this desolation continued during the whole of the reign of Amasis, which was just forty years. See Herod. lib. 3 c. 10; and see Calmet.
entries.660e4c7f8355e294c9486fc8dcd40e6d8974d06c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32139" type="x-p"/> Will I gather the Egyptians - It is probable that Cyrus gave permission to the Egyptians brought to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, to return to their own country. And if we reckon from the commencement of the war against Pharaoh-hophra by Nebuchadnezzar, to the third or fourth year of Cyrus, the term will be about forty years.
entries.2f07f029d9f9f96a5a8fdea577d852009f0d7b8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32140" type="x-p"/> Into the land of Pathros - Supposed to mean the Delta, a country included between the branches of the Nile, called Δ delta, from its being in the form of the Greek letter of that name. It may mean the Pathrusim, in Upper Egypt, near to the Thebaid. This is most likely. <div eID="gen32140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32141" type="x-p"/> Shall be there a base kingdom - That is, it shall continue to be tributary. It is upwards of two thousand years since this prophecy was delivered, and it has been uninterruptedly fulfilling to the present hour. <div eID="gen32141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32142" type="x-p"/> 1. Egypt became tributary to the Babylonians under Amasis. <div eID="gen32142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32143" type="x-p"/> 2. After the ruin of the Babylonish empire, it became subject to the Persians. <div eID="gen32143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32144" type="x-p"/> 3. After the Persians, it came into the hands of the Macedonians. <div eID="gen32144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32145" type="x-p"/> 4. After the Macedonians it fell into the hands of the Romans. <div eID="gen32145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32146" type="x-p"/> 5. After the division of the Roman empire it was subdued by the Saracens. <div eID="gen32146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32147" type="x-p"/> 6. About a.d. 1250, it came into the hands of the Mameluke slaves. <div eID="gen32147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32148" type="x-p"/> 7. Selim, the ninth emperor of the Turks, conquered the Mamelukes, a.d. 1517, and annexed Egypt to the Ottoman empire, of which it still continues to be a province, governed by a pacha and twenty-four beys, who are always advanced from servitude to the administration of public affairs. So true is it that Egypt, once so glorious, is the basest of kingdoms. See Newton on the prophecies.
entries.09f2bd50aa648f3978739f597e15204316cce555: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32149" type="x-p"/> The seven and twentieth year - That is, of the captivity of Jeconiah, fifteen years after the taking of Jerusalem; about April 20, 3432. The preceding prophecy was delivered one year before the taking of Jerusalem; this, sixteen years after; and it is supposed to be the last which this prophet wrote.
entries.c1f19486f880efe1238c50253c7ff82b99c5c61b: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32150" type="x-p"/> Caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus - He was thirteen years employed in the siege. See Joseph. Antiq. lib. 10 c. 11. In this siege his soldiers endured great hardships. Being continually on duty, their heads became bald by wearing their helmets; and their shoulders bruised and peeled by carrying baskets of earth to the fortifications, and wood, etc., to build towers, etc. <div eID="gen32150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32151" type="x-p"/> Yet had he no wages, nor his army - The Tyrians, finding it at last impossible to defend their city, put all their wealth aboard their vessels, sailed out of the port, and escaped for Carthage; and thus Nebuchadnezzar lost all the spoil of one of the richest cities in the world.
entries.35f9e36627d656580df95b1bd5349d157851d433: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32152" type="x-p"/> I have given him the land of Egypt for his labor - Because he fulfilled the designs of God against Tyre, God promises to reward him with the spoil of Egypt.
entries.6e9897e69d16657ba576d7265740fed8eda1fd5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32153" type="x-p"/> Will I cause the horn of the house of Israel to bud - This may refer generally to the restoration; but particularly to Zerubbabel, who became one of the leaders of the people from Babylon. Or it may respect Daniel, or Mordecai, or Jeconiah, who, about this time, was brought out of prison by Evil-merodach, and afterwards kindly treated.  <chapter eID="Ezek.29"/> <div eID="gen32153" type="x-p"/>

entries.1ab6d198fa8a3569f31ba0fcdb4899130e9b0673: <div eID="gen15075" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Against Egypt - Ezekiel 29-32</title> <div sID="gen15076" type="x-p"/> The announcement of the judgment upon Egypt is proclaimed in seven “words of God.” The first five are threats. The first (Ezekiel 29:1-16) contains a threat of the judgment upon Pharaoh and his people and land, expressed in grand and general traits. The second (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:17-21</reference>) gives a special prediction of the conquest and plundering of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar. The third (Ezekiel 30:1-19) depicts the day of judgment which will break upon Egypt and its allies. The fourth (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20-Ezek.30.26">Eze 30:20-26</reference>) foretells the annihilation of the might of Pharaoh by the king of Babylon; and the fifth (Ezekiel 31) holds up as a warning to the king and people of Egypt the glory and the overthrow of Assyria. The last two words of God in Ezekiel 32 contain lamentations over the destruction of Pharaoh and his might, viz., Ezekiel 32:1-16, a lamentation over the king of Egypt; and Ezekiel 32:17-32, a second lamentation over the destruction of his imperial power. - Ezekiel’s prophecy concerning Egypt assumes this elaborate form, because he regards the power of Pharaoh and Egypt as the embodiment of that phase of the imperial power which imagines in its ungodly self-deification that it is able to uphold the kingdom of God, and thus seduces the people of God to rely with false confidence upon the imperial power of this world. <div eID="gen15076" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment upon Pharaoh and His People and Land</title> <div sID="gen15077" type="x-p"/> Because Pharaoh looks upon himself as the creator of his kingdom and of his might, he is to be destroyed with his men of war (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.2-Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:2-5</reference></hi>). In order that Israel may no longer put its trust in the fragile power of Egypt, the sword shall cut off from Egypt both man and beast, the land shall be turned into a barren wilderness, and the people shall be scattered over the lands (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5-Ezek.29.12">Eze 29:5-12</reference>). But after the expiration of the time appointed for its punishment, both people and land shall be restored, though only to remain an insignificant kingdom (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.13-Ezek.29.16">Eze 29:13-16</reference>). - According to <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1">Eze 29:1</reference>, this prophecy belongs to the tenth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin; and as we may see by comparing it with the other oracles against Egypt of which the dates are given, it was the first word of God uttered by Ezekiel concerning this imperial kingdom. The contents also harmonize with this, inasmuch as the threat which it contains merely announces in general terms the overthrow of the might of Egypt and its king, without naming the instrument employed to execute the judgment, and at the same time the future condition of Egypt is also disclosed. <div eID="gen15077" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Destruction of the might of Pharaoh, and devastation of Egypt</title> <div sID="gen15078" type="x-p"/> Eze 29:1. <hi type="italic">In the tenth year, in the tenth (month), on the twelfth of the month, the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 29:2. <hi type="italic">Son of man, direct thy face against Pharaoh the king of Egypt, and prophesy against him and against all Egypt.</hi> Eze 29:3. <hi type="italic">Speak and say, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Behold, I will deal with thee, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, thou great dragon which lieth in its rivers, which saith, “Mine is the river, and I have made it for myself.”</hi> Eze 29:4. <hi type="italic">I will put a ring into thy jaws, and cause the fishes of thy rivers to hang upon thy scales, and draw thee out of thy rivers, and all the fishes of thy rivers which hang upon thy scales;</hi> Eze 29:5. <hi type="italic">And will cast thee into the desert, thee and all the fishes of thy rivers; upon the surface of the field wilt thou fall, thou wilt not be lifted up nor gathered together; I give thee for food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heaven.</hi> Eze 29:6. <hi type="italic">And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall learn that I am Jehovah. Because it is a reed-staff to the house of Israel, -</hi> Eze 29:7. <hi type="italic">When they grasp thee by thy branches, thou crackest and tearest open all their shoulder; and when they lean upon thee, thou breakest and causest all their loins to shake, -</hi> Eze 29:8. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Behold, I bring upon thee the sword, and will cut off from thee man and beast;</hi> Eze 29:9. <hi type="italic">And the land of Egypt will become a waste and desolation, and they shall learn that I am Jehovah. Because he saith: “The river is mine, and I have made it,”</hi> Eze 29:10. <hi type="italic">Therefore, behold, I will deal with thee and thy rivers, and will make the land of Egypt into barren waste desolations from Migdol to Syene, even to the border of Cush.</hi> Eze 29:11. <hi type="italic">The foot of man will not pass through it, and the foot of beast will not pass through it, and it will not be inhabited for forty years.</hi> Eze 29:12. <hi type="italic">I make the land of Egypt a waste in the midst of devastated lands, and its cities shall be waste among desolate cities forty years; and I scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them in the lands.</hi> - The date given, viz., “in the tenth year,” is defended even by Hitzig as more correct than the reading of the lxx, ἐν τῷ ἔτει τῷ δωδεκάτω; and he supposes the Alexandrian reading to have originated in the fact that the last date mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.1">Eze 26:1</reference> had already brought down the account to the eleventh year. - Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, against whom the threat is first directed, is called “the great dragon” in Eze 29:3. תּנּים (here and <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">Eze 32:2</reference>) is equivalent to תּנּין, literally, the lengthened animal, the snake; here, the water-snake, the crocodile, the standing symbol of Egypt in the prophets (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.13">Psa 74:13</reference>), which is here transferred to Pharaoh, as the ruler of Egypt and representative of its power. By יארים we are to understand the arms and canals of the Nile (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference>). The predicate, “lying in the midst of his rivers,” points at once to the proud security in his own power to which Pharaoh gave himself up. As the crocodile lies quietly in the waters of the Nile, as though he were lord of the river; so did Pharaoh regard himself as the omnipotent lord of Egypt. His words affirm this: “the river is mine, I have made it for myself.” The suffix attached to עשׂיתני stands in the place of לי, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.9">Eze 29:9</reference>, where the suffix is wanting, clearly shows. There is an incorrectness in this use of the suffix, which evidently passed into the language of literature from the popular phraseology (cf. Ewald, §315 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The rendering of the Vulgate, <hi type="italic">ego feci memetipsum</hi>, is false. יארי is the expression used by him as a king who regards the land and its rivers as his own property; in connection with which we must bear in mind that Egypt is indebted to the Nile not only for its greatness, but for its actual existence. In this respect Pharaoh says emphatically לי, it is mine, it belongs to me, because he regards himself as the creator. The words, “I have made it for myself,” simply explain the reason for the expression לי, and affirm more than “I have put myself in possession of this through my own power, or have acquired its blessings for myself” (Hävernick); or, “I have put it into its present condition by constructing canals, dams, sluices, and buildings by the river-side” (Hitzig). Pharaoh calls himself the creator of the Nile, because he regards himself as the creator of the greatness of Egypt. This pride, in which he forgets God and attributes divine power to himself, is the cause of his sin, for which he will be overthrown by God. God will draw the crocodile Pharaoh out of his Nile with hooks, and cast him upon the dry land, where he and the fishes that have been drawn out along with him upon his scales will not be gathered up, but devoured by the wild beasts and birds of prey. The figure is derived from the manner in which even in ancient times the crocodile was caught with large hooks of a peculiar construction (compare Herod. ii. 70, and the testimonies of travellers in Oedmann’s <hi type="italic">Vermischten Sammlungen</hi>, III pp. 6ff., and Jomard in the <hi type="italic">Déscription de l'Egypte</hi>, I p. 27). The form חחיים with a double <hi type="italic">Yod</hi> is a copyist’s error, probably occasioned by the double <hi type="italic">Yod</hi> occurring after ח in בּלחייך, which follows. A dual form for חחים is unsuitable, and is not used anywhere else even by Ezekiel (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.4">Eze 19:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.9">Eze 19:9</reference>, and more especially <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.4">Eze 38:4</reference>). <div eID="gen15078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15079" type="x-p"/> The fishes which hang upon the scales of the monster, and are drawn along with it out of the Nile, are the inhabitants of Egypt, for the Nile represents the land. The casting of the beast into the wilderness, where it putrefies and is devoured by the beasts and birds of prey, must not be interpreted in the insipid manner proposed by Hitzig, namely, that Pharaoh would advance with his army into the desert of Arabia and be defeated there. The wilderness is the dry and barren land, in which animals that inhabit the water must perish; and the thought is simply that the monster will be cast upon the desert land, where it will finally become the food of the beasts of prey. <div eID="gen15079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15080" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.6">Eze 29:6</reference> the construction is a subject of dispute, inasmuch as many of the commentators follow the Hebrew division of the verse, taking the second hemistich 'יען היותם וגו as dependent upon the first half of the verse, for which it assigns the reason, and then interpreting <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.7">Eze 29:7</reference> as a further development of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.6">Eze 29:6</reference></hi>, and commencing a new period with <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.8">Eze 29:8</reference> (Hitzig, Kliefoth, and others). But it is decidedly wrong to connect together the two halves of the sixth verse, if only for the simple reason that the formula וידעוּ כּי אני יהוה, which occurs so frequently elsewhere in Ezekiel, invariably closes a train of thought, and is never followed by the addition of a further reason. Moreover, a sentence commencing with יען is just as invariably followed by an apodosis introduced by לכן, of which we have an example just below in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.9">Eze 29:9</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">Eze 29:10</reference></hi>. For both these reasons it is absolutely necessary that we should regard 'יען ה as the beginning of a protasis, the apodosis to which commences with לכן in Eze 29:8. The correctness of this construction is established beyond all doubt by the fact that from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.6">Eze 29:6</reference></hi> onwards it is no longer Pharaoh who is spoken of, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3-Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:3-5</reference>, but Egypt; so that יען introduces a new train of thought. But <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.7">Eze 29:7</reference> is clearly shown, both by the contents and the form, to be an explanatory intermediate clause inserted as a parenthesis. And inasmuch as the protasis is removed in consequence to some distance from its apodosis, Ezekiel has introduced the formula “thus saith the Lord Jehovah” at the commencement of the apodosis, for the purpose of giving additional emphasis to the announcement of the punishment. <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.7">Eze 29:7</reference> cannot in any case be regarded as the protasis, the apodosis to which commences with the לכן in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.8">Eze 29:8</reference>, and Hävernick maintains. The suffix attached to היותם, to which Hitzig takes exception, because he has misunderstood the construction, and which he would conjecture away, refers to מצרים as a land or kingdom. Because the kingdom of Egypt was a reed-staff to the house of Israel (a figure drawn from the physical character of the banks of the Nile, with its thick growth of tall, thick rushes, and recalling to mind <reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">Isa 36:6</reference>), the Lord would bring the sword upon it and cut off from it both man and beast. But before this apodosis the figure of the reed-staff is more clearly defined: “when they (the Israelites) take thee by thy branches, thou breakest,” etc. This explanation is not to be taken as referring to any particular facts either of the past or future, but indicates the deceptive nature of Egypt as the standing characteristic of that kingdom. At the same time, to give greater vivacity to the description, the words concerning Egypt are changed into a direct address to the Egyptians, i.e., not to Pharaoh, but to the Egyptian people regarded as a single individual. The expression בכפך causes some difficulty, since the ordinary meaning of כּף (hand) is apparently unsuitable, inasmuch as the verb תּרוץ, from רצץ, to break or crack (not to break in pieces, i.e., to break quite through), clearly shows that the figure if the reed is still continued. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> בּכּף is a bad emendation, based upon the rendering “to grasp with the hand,” which is grammatically inadmissible. תּפשׂ with ב does not mean to grasp with something, but to seize upon something, to take hold of a person (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.6">Isa 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.17">Deu 9:17</reference>), so that בכפך can only be an explanatory apposition to בּך. The meaning grip, or grasp of the hand, is also unsuitable and cannot be sustained, as the plural כּפּות alone is used in this sense in Sol 5:5. The only meaning appropriate to the figure is that of branches, which is sustained, so far as the language is concerned, by the use of the plural כּפּות for palm-branches in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev 23:40</reference>, and of the singular כּפּה for the collection of branches in <reference osisRef="Job.15.32">Job 15:32</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Isa 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.15">Isa 19:15</reference>; and this is apparently in perfect harmony with natural facts, since the tall reed of the Nile, more especially the papyrus, is furnished with hollow, sword-shaped leaves at the lower part of the talk. When it cracks, the reed-staff pierces the shoulder of the man who has grasped it, and tears it; and if a man lean upon it, it breaks in pieces and causes all the loins to tremble. העמיד cannot mean to cause to stand, or to set upright, still less render stiff and rigid. The latter meaning cannot be established from the usage of the language, and would be unsuitable here. For if a stick on which a man leans should break and penetrate his loins, it would inflict such injury upon them as to cause him to fall, and not to remain stiff and rigid. העמד cannot have any other meaning than that of המעד, to cause to tremble or relax, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.24">Psa 69:24</reference>, to shake the firmness of the loins, so that the power to stand is impaired. <div eID="gen15080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15081" type="x-p"/> In the apodosis the thought of the land gives place to that of the people; hence the use of the feminine suffixes עליך and ממּך in the place of the masculine suffixes בּך and עליך in Eze 29:7. Man and beast shall be cut off, and the land made into a desert waste by the sword, i.e., by war. This is carried out still further in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.9-Ezek.29.12">Eze 29:9-12</reference>; and once again in the protasis 9 <hi type="italic">b</hi> (cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference></hi>) the inordinate pride of the king is placed in the foreground as the reason for the devastation of his land and kingdom. The Lord will make of Egypt the most desolate wilderness. חרבות is intensified into a superlative by the double genitive חרב שׁממה, desolation of the wilderness. Throughout its whole extent from <hi type="italic">Migdol</hi>, i.e., Magdolo, according to the <hi type="italic">Itiner. Anton.</hi> p. 171 (ed. Wessel), twelve Roman miles from Pelusium; in the Coptic <hi type="italic">Meshtol</hi>, Egyptian <hi type="italic">Màktr</hi> (Brugsch, <hi type="italic">Geogr. Inschr.</hi> I pp. 261f.), the most northerly place in Egypt. סונה, to Syene (for the construction see <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">Eze 30:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.3">Eze 21:3</reference>), Συήνη, <hi type="italic">Sun</hi> in the inscriptions, according to Brugsch (<hi type="italic">Geogr. Inschr.</hi> I. p. 155), probably the profane designation of the place (Coptic <hi type="italic">Souan</hi>), the most southerly border town of Egypt in the direction of Cush, i.e., Ethiopia, on the eastern bank of the Nile, some ruins of which are still to be seen in the modern <hi type="italic">Assvan</hi> (<hi type="italic">Assuan</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">aswa=n</hi>), which is situated to the north-east of them (vid., Brugsch, <hi type="italic">Reiseber</hi>. <hi type="italic">aus</hi>. <hi type="italic">Aegypten</hi>, p. 247, and Leyrer in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Encyclopaedia</hi>). The additional clause, “and to the border of Cush,” does not give a fresh terminal point, still further advanced, but simply defines with still greater clearness the boundary toward the south, viz., to Syene, where Egypt terminates and Ethiopia beings. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.11">Eze 29:11</reference></hi> the desolation is more fully depicted. לא תשׁב, it will not dwell, poetical for “be inhabited,” as in Joel 4 (3):20, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">Isa 13:20</reference>, etc. This devastation shall last for forty years, and so long shall the people of Egypt be scattered among the nations. But after the expiration of that time they shall be gathered together again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.13">Eze 29:13</reference>). The number forty is neither a round number (Hitzig) nor a very long time (Ewald), but is a symbolical term denoting a period appointed by God for punishment and penitence (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.6">Eze 4:6</reference>), which is not to be understood in a chronological sense, or capable of being calculated.
